1.explanation: The core of the problem lives in the object array passed to `Prism.languages.insertBefore('ruby','keyword',…)`. The first entry (for `%r{…}`) includes an `inside: { interpolation: interpolation }` definition so that `#{…}` is tokenized correctly. The second entry — the slash-delimited regex matcher — omits any `inside` property, so interpolations in `/…/` never get their own token. To fix the bug, the slash pattern must be extended with the same `inside: { interpolation: interpolation }` block used by the `%r` matcher.
1.bug_scenario: On the Prism.js test page with Ruby selected, slash-delimited regex literals that contain interpolation — e.g. `/foo#{bar}/` — render as a single token and do not highlight the `#{bar}` portion, whereas the equivalent `%r[...]` form correctly highlights the interpolation.

2.explanation: The variable interpolation defines the rules for #{…} interpolation and is wired up correctly in the %r{…} regex pattern (the first object in the regex array). However, the second pattern—matching slash-delimited regex—has no “inside: { interpolation }” property, so interpolation is never applied there. To fix the bug, the slash-pattern object in the Prism.languages.insertBefore('ruby','keyword',{ regex: [...] }) call must be extended to include the interpolation token in its inside map, just like the %r pattern does.
2.bug_scenario: On the PrismJS Ruby test page, interpolation inside a percent-style regex (e.g. %r[foo#{bar}]) is highlighted correctly, but interpolation inside a slash-delimited regex (e.g. /foo#{bar}/) is not. The screenshot shows that in the slash form, “#{bar}” is treated as plain text, whereas in the %r form it is tokenized as interpolation.
